extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and writers of cultural/social criticism (Victorian-era and modern), students of literature and social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing cultural/social criticism essays that argue for culture as the pursuit of human perfection (beauty and intelligence — 'sweetness and light'), balancing thought and action and judging institutions by their contribution to human perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as pursuit of perfection (sweetness and light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is, or ought to be, the study and pursuit of perfection; the main characters of that perfection are beauty and intelligence — in other words 'sweetness and light'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'sweetness' (beauty, humane feeling) and 'light' (intelligence, enlightened judgment) together as the defining measures of perfection. The pursuit of culture aims to make reason and the will of God prevail, and ultimately to extend sweetness and light to as many people as possible. Anti-patterns: treating aesthetics or intellect in isolation or elevating machinery/achievement as the end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test organisations by an ideal of human perfection complete on all sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture and poetry test organisations (religious, political, social) by the ideal of a human perfection complete on all sides rather than by their partial virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutions, judge not only the particular faults they correct (e.g., Puritanism's moral strictness) but whether their overall conception of human perfection is broad and humane. Examples: religious organisations that helped subdue animal faults but hold a narrow ideal; the Nonconformist life (jealousy of Establishment, tea-meetings) is inadequate as a full ideal. Avoid explaining away institutional shortcomings by religious jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include moral practice alongside aesthetic and intellectual ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of culture must not neglect moral virtues; culture's ideals should include actual moral practice, not only appreciation of beauty or intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that cultured people may fail in morality and that such failure is punished; insist that morality is indispensable. Balance aesthetic/intellectual aspirations with the cultivation and demonstration of moral virtue. Anti-pattern: excusing aesthetic/intellectual failings by disparaging practical morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat large movements as 'machinery' — necessary but not to be worshipped
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements like wealth, industrialism, muscular Christianity, political organisations, and religious organisations are 'machinery' — they can be necessary preparations but should not be admired as ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the instrumental value of these movements (e.g., industrialism may lay material foundations for the future) while criticizing how they sacrifice present generations and harden people into Philistinism. Avoid the idolatry of machinery: evaluate movements by the ultimate ends they serve (sweetness and light), not by their own momentum or achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and avoidance of fanaticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture demands flexibility — a refusal to be fanatical — seeing tendencies as potentially salutary yet subject to criticism if they outlive their purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to accept the temporary necessity of certain tendencies (e.g., sports, industrialism) while pointing out their mischiefs and guarding against their becoming permanent idols. Culture's flexibility enables criticism without destructive fanaticism; anti-patterns include Jacobin fierceness and imposition of a single abstract system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise 'light' (enlightenment) before action to avoid ill-regulated activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Before advocating or joining in rough, coarse, or ill-regulated action, cultivate and supply 'light' (intelligence, understanding) so action will be effective and not merely random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue for laying in a stock of light to qualify and direct action: refusing to act at any price can be the most practical line when current action is misguided. Use examples where hasty action without sufficient thought causes mischief. Anti-pattern: valorising mere activity ('doing something') without the guiding intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffuse culture by humanising knowledge, not by teaching down
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture seeks to make the best knowledge accessible and humanised for all, but without condescending popularisation or doctrinal indoctrination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to 'divest knowledge of all that was harsh, uncouth, difficult, abstract, professional, exclusive' so it can be effective outside the cultivated clique, yet still remain the best knowledge. Avoid 'teaching down' or reducing ideas to ready-made watchwords; do not attempt to indoctrinate the masses with party or professional creeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: The social idea: culture as an apostle of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of culture are true apostles of equality because they work to diffuse the best knowledge and ideas across society, breaking down class barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure cultural work by its success in broadening the basis of life and intelligence, and in making sweetness and light widespread. Examples: figures like Abelard, Lessing, and Herder humanised knowledge and diffused culture. Anti-pattern: confining culture to an elite clique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject idolising leaders or systems ('Be not ye called Rabbi!')
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture resists the elevation of any one man or system into the final arbiter of progress; it prefers to follow currents and resist fixed 'Rabbi' authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing movements or thinkers (Bentham, Comte, Buckle, Mill), acknowledge merits but remember their limitations and do not make them unquestioned rulers of society. Jacobinism's love of a Rabbi and abstract systems is to be criticized; culture continually passes onward in pursuit of further perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge reforms and achievements by their contribution to sweetness and light, not by mere material success
rubrics_metrics.description: Political or industrial achievements (e.g., railroads, manufactures, franchises) are insufficient measures of human perfection unless they increase sweetness and light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist rhetoric that equates national greatness with material or institutional accomplishments. Instead, ask whether such achievements foster increased spiritual activity, sympathy, beauty, and intelligence. Beware of teaching people to value themselves merely by material accomplishments; that trains new Philistines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and critique the sacrificial cost of necessary tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit that certain necessary movements (industrialism, Puritanism, Nonconformity, athletic training) may benefit the future but sacrifice the present generation's harmonious perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out who is being 'sacrificed' (passing generations of industrialists, boys in games, Puritans) and argue culture should criticise such mischiefs to prevent permanent hardening. Use this as grounds for cultural intervention and for tempering blind praise of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperate judgment: severe on actions, merciful on persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture combines a severe judgment of actions with a merciful judgment of persons, showing indulgence and understanding of circumstances while condemning harmful deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an attitude that resists fierce wholesale condemnation (Jacobin hatred of the past) while still holding individuals and systems accountable for actions. This balanced stance allows criticism of mistakes without personal vilification and helps preserve the pursuit of perfection.
